**TREC — the benchmark that was incomplete by construction, and useful anyway (1994–2004)**

NIST's Text REtrieval Conference met the problem every evaluation harness eventually meets: ground truth cannot be exhaustive. Ad hoc collections ran to hundreds of thousands of documents, and judging each against every topic was unaffordable. TREC's answer was pooling — take the top 100 documents from each participating run, union them, have a human assessor judge only that pool, and score everything unjudged as non-relevant. The scoring pipeline was therefore built on a dataset known to be incomplete, and the question was never whether it was wrong but whether it was wrong in a way that changed decisions.

Zobel's 1998 study "How reliable are the results of large-scale information retrieval experiments?" tested that with leave-out-one-run experiments: rebuild the pool without a system's own contribution, then re-score it against the diminished judgements. At pool depth 100 on the newswire collections the comparisons held; downsampling showed substantial degradation at depth 10 but not at depth 50. Buckley and Voorhees later mapped where that breaks: as collections grow, a fixed-size pool covers a shrinking fraction of the corpus, and surviving judgements skew towards documents containing the topic's title words. The collection stays reusable for systems resembling those that built the pool, and penalises those that do not.

The judges were no better. Voorhees had three assessors independently judge the TREC-4 topics and measured the overlap between their relevant sets at between 0.301 and 0.494 — agreement on well under half. An independent label set for TREC-6 reached a Cohen's kappa of only 0.52 against the official one. Absolute scores moved accordingly. Yet re-ranking the systems under each assessor's judgements gave a mean Kendall's tau against the official TREC ranking of 0.938, and the TREC-6 comparison came out at 0.8956.

Those are two guarantees, and TREC only ever offered the second. The absolute number a system reported was an artefact of who judged and how deep the pool went; the ordering was robust to both. Two decades of retrieval progress were measured on a ruler nobody trusted to be accurate, because it was trusted to be monotone.

Your harness inherits that shape exactly. An LLM judge that agrees with your human labellers half the time is not disqualifying if the ranking it induces over candidate agents is stable, so measure that: rank correlation across judge seeds, rubrics and orderings, rather than agreement as the target. And treat pooling bias as live: an eval set mined from your current agent's traces is a pool built by one system, and it will under-credit a replacement that succeeds by a route today's agent never takes.

**Optimizely — the dashboard that rewarded you for looking (2015)**

Every experimentation platform ships a results page, and every results page invites the same behaviour: refresh, watch the significance figure, stop when it crosses. On 20 January 2015 Optimizely published the reasoning behind its new Stats Engine, and the unusual thing about that post is how much of it is an indictment of the product's own previous default.

The measurements are blunt. In simulated A/A tests — two identical variants, no effect to find — monitoring after every visitor and stopping at the first p below 0.05 declared a winner 57% of the time. Peeking on a coarser schedule only partly helped: checking every 500 visitors produced false declarations around 26% of the time, every 1,000 visitors around 20%. A second inflation came from breadth rather than from time. Five variations against two goals each yielded a false discovery ratio near 50% while the per-comparison error rate was nominally controlled at 10%.

Stats Engine attacked both. Sequential testing built on continuously updated likelihood ratios produced always-valid p-values, so the reported result is legitimate at whatever moment the experimenter chooses to stop; Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control was applied across variations and goals, changing the guarantee into a statement about the whole set of declared winners and losers rather than about any single comparison. Replayed over 48,000 historical experiments from Optimizely's own customers, the simulated false positive rate fell from over 20% to under 5%, and the share of declarations that later reversed fell from 44% to 6%.

The bill was paid in throughput. Conclusive results dropped from 36% of experiments to 22%, and Optimizely reported that roughly 80% of the tests that stopped being called were underpowered — they had never earned their conclusions in the first place. Harder for adoption: an experiment whose true lift lands exactly on the pre-specified minimum detectable effect runs up to about 60% slower than a correctly sized fixed-horizon test. Sequential methods win the speed argument only when the real effect is larger than you planned for.

Agent experiments make peeking harder to resist than web experiments do, because each observation costs real money and the canary dashboard is open anyway. Choose the regime before you start: a fixed horizon with a pre-registered sample size and genuine discipline about not looking, or a sequential boundary whose price you accept in run length. And count your comparisons honestly. An agent change is almost never judged on one number, and the accuracy, latency, cost and safety panels on your dashboard are four looks per refresh, not one.

**Canopy — 1.3 billion traces a day, and a regression no single trace could show (2017)**

Canopy is the end-to-end tracing system Facebook's engineers described at SOSP 2017. It records causally related performance events across the whole path of a request — browser and mobile clients, web tier, backend services — and at publication was generating and processing about 1.3 billion traces per day, roughly 1.16 Gb/s of event data, backing 129 derived performance datasets. Not everything is recorded: a distributed token-bucket scheme rate-limits tracing globally and per tenant, and engineers can supply custom policies to target requests with particular properties.

The paper's worked example is a regression from March 2017. The average time to display the initial portion of one page rose by 300 ms, about 13%. Broken down by component, server execution time and network time were essentially unchanged, while browser execution time and resource-fetching time had both risen. The symptom lived in the client.

Following it back across the boundary took three further steps. Resource prediction accuracy had fallen by about 5%. The reason was an extra 10 kB of CSS being sent in the early-flush payload, which displaced resources the client actually needed and left the browser waiting on fetches it should already have had in hand. Per-component attribution put the CSS increase on the UserInput component, and the fix was a reconfiguration of the early flush mechanism. Nothing in that chain had errored. Every service returned success, and the cause sat several boundaries away from the symptom.

Two design consequences follow, and the paper is candid about both. First, a 13% shift sits inside per-request noise, so no individual trace shows it — which is why Canopy is built as a feature-extraction and aggregation pipeline rather than a trace viewer, and why the features have to be decided at ingest. Second, the trace model itself was got wrong repeatedly: an RPC-centric representation could not express time spent blocked waiting for a response, forcing a move to execution units, then client-queue events, then an edge-based model. The instrumentation schema, not the storage, was the hard part.

Your agent traces have the same topology — a tree spanning a model provider, a retriever, several tool APIs and a client, any of which can return 200 while degrading the whole. If your observability practice amounts to opening a slow trace, you will find outliers and miss regressions. Decide now which features every trace emits: LLM latency fraction, tool-call and iteration counts, token totals against the context budget, stop reasons. Those are what a regression becomes visible in, and you cannot compute them later on the traces your sampler threw away.

**British Airways — seventy-five days of successful transactions (2018–2020)**

On 22 June 2018 an attacker signed in to British Airways' systems with the credentials of a Swissport employee — a supplier account holding legitimate access and, contrary to BA's own network access policy, no multi-factor authentication in front of it. Within days the attacker held privileged domain administrator credentials, obtained in part from a file where a username and password sat in plain text. By late July they had reached files of payment card details written in the clear since December 2015 by what the Information Commissioner's Office later called a testing feature left switched on in the live environment. In August they added twenty-two lines of JavaScript to the payment pages, copying customers' card data to a domain of their own.

Nothing failed. The site kept serving pages, the payment flow kept completing, and every transaction succeeded. BA learned of it on 5 September, when a third party reported unusual traffic leaving the site. That is seventy-five days from initial access to detection, and the detection did not come from BA.

What followed was quick: the malicious script was removed within about ninety minutes, and the regulator and affected customers were notified the next day. The ICO put the number of individuals whose data was accessible at approximately 429,612, including around 244,000 whose card numbers, expiry dates and security codes were taken.

The penalty notice of 16 October 2020 is the document worth reading, and the fine — £20 million, cut from the £183.39 million notice of intent of July 2019 — matters least. The regulator's findings turn on detection rather than on the intrusion: the controls that would have caught this were available, unexceptional and absent. Multi-factor authentication on remote access. Restriction of privileged accounts. Rigorous testing. Monitoring that would have flagged a changed payment script and an outbound destination nobody recognised. Mitigation took ninety minutes; it was preceded by seventy-five days of nobody looking.

This is the shape of the agent incident to fear most, and your severity matrix already concedes the point: the SEV-0 case is not the one that pages you, it is the one where the agent returns 200 OK and does harm anyway. Ninety-minute mitigations are cheap to write into a runbook and worth close to nothing if the clock never starts. Put the effort into the detectors that start it — alerts on tool calls to destinations outside your allowlist, on output shapes that changed without a deploy, on a canary transaction that verifies behaviour instead of availability — and rehearse the question the post-incident review opens with: how would we have found this if nobody had told us?

**Windows Error Reporting — ten years of letting the field set the backlog (1999–2009)**

WER shipped with Windows XP, and by the time its authors described it at SOSP 2009 the client code ran on approximately one billion machines — every Windows release since XP, Windows Mobile, Microsoft programs on the Macintosh, and Windows Live JavaScript in any browser — having collected billions of error reports in ten years of operation. It is the largest documented feedback loop from production failures back into a development backlog, and the decisions it made are the decisions any continuous improvement pipeline faces.

The central mechanism is bucketing. A report is not a bug, it is evidence about one, so WER assigns each incoming report to a bucket meant to correspond to a single defect. Two families of heuristics do the work, pulling in opposite directions: expanding heuristics split buckets so that two distinct bugs do not share one, and condensing heuristics merge buckets so that reports from a single bug do not scatter. Once bucketed, the count becomes the prioritisation signal — programmers sort by volume and start at the top, because report volume is the closest available proxy for users affected.

That works only because the distribution is savagely skewed, and the paper shows it: for the Office 2010 internal technical preview, the last quartile of error reports is spread across 88% to 93% of the buckets. Almost every bucket is irrelevant by volume; a handful carry nearly all the users. The pay-off is concrete: the Windows Vista team found and fixed over 5,000 bugs isolated by WER during the beta, prioritised by a ranking no internal test pass could produce.

The costs are equally concrete. A billion machines cannot each upload a full memory dump, so collection is progressive: a minimal report first, with broader dumps, registry values, log files and instrumentation output requested only for buckets that earn the bandwidth. And the loop is never better than its clustering. Over-condense and two unrelated defects contend for one queue position; over-expand and a single defect smears across buckets, none large enough to schedule. The heuristics are explicitly heuristics, and the ranked backlog inherits their errors.

All of that maps onto the pipeline you are building. Agent failures also arrive as evidence, not diagnoses, and they have to be clustered before they can be counted — which makes the bucket key a design decision, not an implementation detail: failing tool name, terminal state, retrieved-document set, an embedding of the trajectory. Choose it deliberately, promote the largest buckets into permanent regression cases in the eval suite, and spend expensive detail — full traces, judge scores, human review — only on buckets that earn it.
